title: Zeno's Paradoxes: How Can Motion Be Impossible?
question: If you must cross half a distance before crossing the whole of it, and half of that half before that, how does anyone ever arrive anywhere?
summary: Twenty-five centuries ago, Zeno of Elea argued that motion is an illusion by chopping any journey into an infinite number of steps. The paradox looks childish until you try to say exactly why it's wrong.
content:
Around 450 BCE, a Greek philosopher named Zeno set out to defend his teacher Parmenides' claim that change and motion are illusions, by showing that the alternative — a world where things actually move — leads to absurdity. His most famous argument, the Dichotomy, is deceptively simple: before you can walk across a room, you must first walk halfway across it. But before you can cover that half, you must cover half of that half. And before that, half of that. The sequence never bottoms out. To go anywhere, Zeno argued, you would first have to complete an infinite number of tasks — which seems impossible. Therefore motion is impossible. And yet, obviously, people cross rooms all the time.

The trick that isn't quite a trick

The standard modern rebuttal is that Zeno's infinite sequence of distances (1/2, 1/4, 1/8, ...) sums to a finite total, 1, and that a finite time can likewise be sliced into infinitely many finite fractions that still add up to a finite duration. Calculus formalizes this as a convergent geometric series. Problem solved — or so it seems in a calculus textbook. But this answer, satisfying as mathematics, sidesteps Zeno's actual worry, which was never about whether the numbers add up. It was about whether an infinite number of discrete acts can be completed at all, even if each act takes vanishingly little time. Summing an infinite series tells you where the limit is; it doesn't obviously tell you how a physical process could complete infinitely many sub-tasks in finite time, a puzzle philosophers now call a "supertask."

The arrow and the illusion of instants

Zeno had a second, nastier paradox: the Arrow. At any single frozen instant, a flying arrow occupies exactly the space equal to its own length — meaning at that instant it is not moving, since motion requires occupying different places at different times, and an instant has no duration in which to move. If the arrow is motionless at every instant of its flight, how can the flight, made entirely of instants, add up to motion? This paradox is arguably harder than the Dichotomy because it doesn't even require infinite subdivision — it attacks the very idea that continuous motion can be built out of a sequence of static snapshots, which is exactly the model physics eventually adopted (position as a function of time, velocity as its derivative).

Why mathematicians, physicists, and philosophers disagree about what was actually solved

Mathematics resolved the *arithmetic* half of Zeno's puzzle in the 19th century with rigorous theories of infinite series and limits. But whether this resolves the *metaphysical* puzzle — whether space and time are genuinely infinitely divisible "all the way down," or are instead granular at some fundamental scale — remains open. Quantum gravity researchers speculate that spacetime may be discrete at the Planck length (about 10⁻³⁵ meters), which would mean Zeno's infinite subdivision simply never happens in reality: there is a smallest unit of distance and time, and the paradox dissolves not through clever math but through physics refusing to let the premise get started.

A puzzle that outlived its target

Parmenides' full-throated denial that anything ever changes convinced almost no one, then or now. But Zeno's paradoxes proved far more durable than the position they were built to defend, because they exposed something genuinely unsettled about the relationship between the continuous and the discrete — a tension that shows up again in the ultraviolet catastrophe, in Turing's halting problem, in debates over whether the universe is a computation. Zeno essentially asked: can infinity be "used up"? Physics, mathematics, and philosophy are still triangulating an answer from three different directions, and none of them fully agrees with the others about what counts as a resolution.

perspectives.title: Mathematics Perspective
perspectives.description: Convergent infinite series (1/2 + 1/4 + 1/8 + ... = 1) show the distances sum to a finite value, and limit theory explains how an infinite process can have a well-defined finite endpoint without ever literally 'finishing' term by term.

perspectives.title: Physics Perspective
perspectives.description: If spacetime is quantized at the Planck scale, infinite divisibility is physically false — there's a smallest possible step, so the infinite regress Zeno describes never actually occurs in the real world.

perspectives.title: Philosophy Perspective
perspectives.description: The 'supertask' literature asks whether completing infinitely many discrete actions in finite time is logically coherent at all, independent of whether the math checks out — a question calculus alone cannot answer.

perspectives.title: Computer Science Perspective
perspectives.description: Zeno's paradox has a direct analogue in 'Zeno behavior' in hybrid dynamical systems, where a simulated or controlled system executes infinitely many discrete events in a finite time window, crashing real-world control software that assumes events are countable.

perspectives.title: History of Science Perspective
perspectives.description: Zeno's paradoxes sat unresolved for over two thousand years until the formal development of limits and set theory in the 1800s gave mathematicians language precise enough to even state what 'infinite sum' meant.

openQuestions: Is spacetime continuous or fundamentally discrete at the smallest scales?
Can an infinite sequence of physical actions ever be truly 'completed,' or only approached?
Does resolving the mathematics of a paradox count as resolving the paradox itself?
Are there other ancient philosophical puzzles waiting on a mathematical tool that hasn't been invented yet?
